unit.name: Influences on Business
unit.subtitle: Technology, ethics, economics, globalisation, law and competition shape every decision businesses make

lessons.title: Technology & Digital Communication
lessons.description: How e-commerce and digital communication reshape how businesses sell, serve and compete today.
lessons.content_html:
Why Technology Matters to Business

Twenty years ago, opening a shop meant renting a high street unit. Today a teenager can launch a global brand from a bedroom. Technology has rewritten the rules of who can trade, how they reach customers, and how quickly a competitor can appear. For every business — from corner-shop bakers to multinationals like ASOS — e-commerce and digital communication are now influences they cannot ignore.

Key Fact

E-commerce lets UK businesses sell 24 hours a day to a worldwide market without needing physical shops. It lowers rent and staffing costs, but raises new costs — website hosting, cyber-security, courier fees and easier price comparison for customers.

E-commerce in Action

E-commerce is selling online through a website or app. It suits any business that can deliver — physical products, streamed films, software, or services booked remotely. ASOS, the UK fashion retailer, operates with no high-street shops at all. Deliveroo, founded in London in 2013, uses an app to connect customers, riders and restaurants. Even traditional businesses like Tesco now earn billions through Tesco.com grocery deliveries.

The benefits are big: a wider customer base, lower fixed costs, and round-the-clock selling. Businesses can collect data on what customers click, add to baskets and abandon — powerful information for marketing. But customers can also compare prices in seconds, which drives margins down and raises the importance of strong branding.

Running a successful online shop is not free. Businesses face website design and hosting costs, payment processing fees, warehousing and courier charges, and ongoing marketing spend on Google and Meta ads. Cyber-security is a growing cost — a single data breach can cost millions and destroy trust overnight.

Returns are another challenge. ASOS estimates that around a third of clothing orders are returned, and every returned parcel eats into profit. Small businesses without the scale of Amazon can struggle to offer free delivery and free returns profitably.

Digital Communication

Digital communication is how businesses talk to their stakeholders — customers, employees, suppliers, shareholders and the public — using digital tools. Email replaces letters, video calls replace flights, and social media replaces much traditional advertising. A small Manchester bakery can reach thousands of potential customers through Instagram for free; a printed leaflet would cost hundreds and reach only a handful of streets.

Social media has become a two-way conversation. Customers post reviews, complaints and praise publicly. A viral TikTok can make a product sell out overnight — the supermarket chain Aldi saw its Cuthbert the Caterpillar cake go viral in 2021 after a spat with Marks & Spencer. But one angry customer tweet can also damage a reputation in hours, especially if it is screenshotted and shared.

Inside a business, tools like Microsoft Teams, Slack and Zoom let staff work from anywhere. Decisions that used to take a week of meetings can be made in an afternoon video call. Cloud file-sharing means a designer in Leeds and a supplier in Vietnam can work on the same document at the same time.

The risks are information overload, blurred work-life boundaries, and the need for training — especially for older staff or in sectors where digital skills are uneven. Businesses also need clear policies on what is shared publicly, because a careless post from an employee can damage the whole brand.

Winners and Losers

Technology rewards businesses that adapt quickly. High street giants like BHS and Debenhams collapsed partly because they were slow to build online offerings while Amazon and ASOS sprinted ahead. Meanwhile, small independent businesses now access tools — Shopify stores, Etsy shops, Mailchimp newsletters — that were once only available to big firms. The barrier to starting a business has dropped sharply.

Key Fact

Digital communication is cheap, fast and two-way — but it is also public. One angry tweet or a leaked email can reach millions before a business has time to respond. Speed cuts both ways.

The overall message is that technology is not a one-off choice but an ongoing influence. Payment apps, AI chatbots, same-day delivery — each new development forces businesses to rethink their operations, costs and customer experience. The businesses that thrive will be the ones that treat technology as an opportunity, not a threat.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When a case study mentions a business using e-commerce or social media, do not just list generic benefits. Apply the point to the business — for a small independent café, Instagram may be cheap advertising but home delivery is a whole new operation with new costs. For 6-mark Analyse answers, build a chain of reasoning: ‘using TikTok means the café reaches younger customers, which increases footfall, which raises revenue without raising rent.’ For 9-mark Justify questions, weigh the digital option against the alternative before giving your verdict.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • E-commerce lets businesses sell 24/7 to a global audience with lower fixed costs, but raises new costs in delivery, returns and cyber-security.
  • Digital communication — email, social media, video calls — is fast, cheap and two-way, but public mistakes travel just as quickly as successes.
  • Technology is a constant influence: businesses that treat it as an ongoing opportunity outperform those that see it as a one-off upgrade.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes e-commerce?
A) Selling goods only in physical shops
B) Buying and selling goods and services using the internet
C) Advertising a business on television
D) Training staff using online videos
practice_questions.marks: B) Buying and selling goods and services using the internet [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘digital communication’.
practice_questions.marks:
The use of digital tools (such as email, social media, messaging apps or video calls) [1 mark] to share information between a business and its stakeholders [1 mark].

Mastering: precise definition using correct business vocabulary.
Secure: accurate meaning with one clear example.
Developing: partial meaning, example missing or vague.
Emerging: definition incorrect or confused with a related term.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which e-commerce can reduce costs for a small UK fashion retailer.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• Identification: e-commerce removes the need to rent a high-street shop [1 mark].
• Development: the retailer saves on rent, business rates and shop-floor staffing costs [1 mark].
• Reasoning: the money saved can be reinvested in stock, marketing or a wider product range, which can raise sales without raising fixed costs [1 mark].

Mastering: identification, development AND a 'because' chain of reasoning.
Secure: identification and clear development.
Developing: correct identification with limited development.
Emerging: vague or incorrect point about e-commerce.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact of social media on a small independent café that has just opened in a city centre.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (accept developed reasoning that draws on one or more factors):
• Low-cost marketing: free Instagram and TikTok posts reach local customers for no spend, which raises awareness and footfall, leading to higher revenue in the early months when budgets are tight.
• Two-way communication: customers can leave reviews and tag the café, creating social proof that attracts new visitors — but negative reviews can spread just as quickly and damage reputation before the owner can respond.
• Data and engagement: insights on which posts perform well helps the owner refine menu photos and offers, which improves conversion from followers to paying customers.
• Risk of overreliance: if the café depends on one platform and an algorithm changes, visibility can drop overnight.

Mastering: developed chains of reasoning using two or more factors, applied to the café, with clear impact on the business.
Secure: a developed chain on one factor plus a supporting point, applied to the café.
Developing: relevant points listed with limited development or weak application.
Emerging: generic statements about social media with no application.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A small bookshop is deciding between two options to grow sales:
Option 1 — Launch an e-commerce website with UK-wide delivery.
Option 2 — Expand marketing through a paid social-media campaign for the existing shop.
Justify which option the bookshop should choose.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
Option 1 (e-commerce):
• Opens a nationwide market, not limited to local footfall, so potential revenue is far higher.
• Allows the shop to trade 24/7, including overnight and weekends.
• Drawback: set-up costs for a website, payment systems, packaging and couriers; returns eat into margin.
Option 2 (paid social-media campaign):
• Cheaper to start — a few hundred pounds can reach thousands locally.
• Builds on an existing loyal customer base and drives repeat visits.
• Drawback: still limited to people within travelling distance of the shop.

Justification must choose one option and weigh it against the other. A strong answer might argue e-commerce is worth the investment because local footfall is finite and books are easy to package; or argue that the paid campaign is safer first because the shop has no online experience and cash flow is tight.

Mastering: clear decision with two developed reasons for the chosen option, weighed against the rejected option, applied to the bookshop.
Secure: decision with one developed reason plus a supporting point and some weighing.
Developing: decision stated with limited reasoning or weak weighing of the alternative.
Emerging: lists pros and cons of both options with no clear decision.
[9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘All UK high-street retailers should shift most of their sales online.’
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
Arguments in support:
• Online sales allow 24/7 trading and a national or global customer base, which can raise revenue far beyond what a single high-street unit can achieve.
• Fixed costs fall — fewer shops means less rent, rates and staffing.
• Data on customer behaviour helps retailers target marketing and personalise offers, increasing conversion.
• Companies that did not adapt, like BHS and Debenhams, collapsed partly because they relied too heavily on physical stores.

Arguments against:
• Many products — fresh food, clothes needing try-on, high-value items — still sell better in store, where customers touch, try and ask questions.
• E-commerce has its own costs: warehousing, couriers, returns, cyber-security.
• Shutting shops damages community presence, staff relationships and brand image.
• ‘Most’ is a strong word — an integrated strategy (click-and-collect, flagship stores plus online) often works better than going mainly online.

Conclusion should introduce a new weighting: for example, it depends on the type of product and the target customer. Fashion and electronics suit a heavy online tilt; fresh food and premium services may not. The most important factor is knowing where the retailer's customers prefer to buy.

Mastering: balanced argument with two developed points on each side, a justified conclusion that introduces a new weighting (‘it depends on...’ or ‘the most important factor is...’).
Secure: balanced argument with some development and a clear conclusion.
Developing: one-sided argument or a conclusion that only summarises earlier points.
Emerging: brief points with no real evaluation or conclusion.
[12 marks]

lessons.title: Ethics, Environment & Sustainability
lessons.description: Trade-offs between doing the right thing and making a profit, and why sustainability is now a business issue.
lessons.content_html:
Doing the Right Thing — at a Price

When Primark found in 2013 that a factory in Bangladesh it bought clothes from had collapsed, killing more than a thousand workers, it faced a choice: keep paying the lowest price for garments or spend more to audit suppliers and improve conditions. When BrewDog set a 2030 carbon-negative target, it agreed to invest heavily in land restoration and renewable energy. These are classic examples of ethical behaviour — doing what stakeholders consider fair and honest, even when it costs more.

Key Fact

Acting ethically usually raises costs — higher wages, better-sourced materials, environmental clean-up — but can also raise revenue and loyalty by winning customers who care. The exam will always ask you to weigh both sides.

The Ethics-Versus-Profit Trade-off

A trade-off is where a business must give up something in one area to gain in another. Paying a UK living wage above the legal minimum raises staff costs — but can cut staff turnover and training costs, and build brand reputation. Switching to recyclable packaging raises material costs — but can attract new customers and avoid future regulation.

Sometimes the ethical choice is profitable in the long run. The outdoor brand Patagonia built its entire identity on environmental responsibility — even running a ‘Don’t Buy This Jacket’ ad — and grew faster than rivals. But in the short run, ethical choices can hit profits and test shareholders’ patience.

In 2015 Volkswagen was caught fitting ‘defeat devices’ to hide the true emissions of its diesel cars. The scandal, known as ‘dieselgate’, cost the firm over thirty billion dollars in fines and lost sales, and damaged its brand for years. In 2020 the UK fashion retailer Boohoo faced accusations that its Leicester suppliers paid staff far below the minimum wage — sales fell, share price dropped sharply, and the company commissioned an independent review.

The message is clear: unethical shortcuts can generate short-term profit, but when the media, regulators or customers find out, the long-term cost usually outweighs the gain.

Environmental Considerations

Every business decision has an environmental footprint. Operations generate traffic congestion (think of Amazon vans on every street), noise and air pollution, and waste that ends up in landfill. Consumers, councils and governments increasingly expect businesses to act on this. Supermarkets charge 5p for carrier bags; Starbucks and Pret offer discounts for reusable cups; Deliveroo is testing electric bikes and cargo cycles for last-mile deliveries.

Recycling is now a standard cost of doing business. Costa Coffee runs cup-recycling schemes; Tesco takes back soft plastic at its stores. Pollution is regulated too — firms that breach emissions rules face fines, and vehicles in UK clean-air zones pay daily charges.

Sustainability means meeting today’s needs without using up resources future generations will need. Global warming has pushed governments to set net-zero targets, which ripple down into business decisions: electric vans, energy-efficient buildings, carbon-offset schemes.

Scarce resources are a further concern. Fish stocks, rare earth metals for electronics, and fresh water are all finite. Businesses that rely on them need long-term plans — otherwise their own inputs run out. McDonald’s, for example, has committed to sourcing fish only from certified sustainable fisheries, protecting its future supply chain.

Costs and Benefits of Ethical and Green Behaviour

Costs include higher-priced raw materials, staff training on new procedures, investment in cleaner technology, and the risk that ethical decisions are used as marketing without real change — known as greenwashing. Customers and regulators are quick to spot and punish this. In 2022 the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority opened investigations into whether major fashion retailers’ ‘sustainable’ labels were accurate.

Benefits include stronger brand reputation, the ability to charge premium prices, better staff retention (employees want to work for responsible firms), and early compliance with future laws. When governments later tighten rules, ethical firms do not need to scramble.

Key Fact

Environmental impacts of business activity include traffic congestion, noise and air pollution, waste sent to landfill, and the use of scarce resources. Sustainable practices aim to reduce each of these without shutting the business down.

Ethics and sustainability are no longer optional extras. They shape what materials a firm uses, how it hires, what it dares to claim in adverts, and how quickly it can react when a new law lands. Businesses that plan for them early pay less and earn more loyalty than those forced to react under pressure.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Ethics questions almost always reward a balanced answer — do not just say ‘being ethical is good’. For Analyse questions, build a chain of reasoning: ‘recyclable packaging raises material costs, which squeezes margin, but attracts eco-conscious customers, which lifts revenue.’ For 12-mark Evaluate questions, the conclusion must introduce a new weighting — for example, ‘it depends on the type of customer’ — not just repeat the points you have already made. Always name a real example where you can.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Ethical behaviour means acting in ways stakeholders see as fair and honest, even when it costs more — the trade-off between ethics and short-term profit is at the heart of every decision.
  • Businesses affect the environment through traffic, pollution, waste and use of scarce resources; recycling, cleaner logistics and green sourcing can cut these impacts.
  • Sustainability is long-term planning — firms that invest early avoid later fines, protect their supply chains, and earn reputation that keeps customers loyal.

practice_questions.text: Explain one way a coffee chain can reduce its environmental impact.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• Identification: offer a discount for customers using reusable cups [1 mark].
• Development: fewer disposable cups are used, reducing waste sent to landfill [1 mark].
• Reasoning: because less packaging is produced and bought, the firm also cuts raw-material costs and builds a reputation for sustainability, which can attract eco-conscious customers [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a UK fashion retailer of adopting a more ethical supply chain.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (accept developed reasoning that draws on one or more factors):
• Higher costs: paying above-minimum wages and auditing factories raises unit costs, which may squeeze profit margins in the short term.
• Brand reputation: ethical sourcing can be promoted in marketing, attracting eco-conscious customers and supporting premium prices, which raises revenue.
• Staff loyalty: ethical firms often find it easier to recruit and keep staff, reducing training costs.
• Risk reduction: auditing suppliers avoids scandals (e.g. Boohoo 2020) that damage reputation and share price.
• Trade-off: short-term profit versus long-term loyalty — the net effect depends on how quickly customers respond.

Mastering: developed chains of reasoning using two or more factors, applied to a fashion retailer.
Secure: a developed chain on one factor plus a supporting point, applied.
Developing: relevant points listed with limited development or weak application.
Emerging: generic statements about ethics with no application.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A medium-sized chocolate manufacturer is choosing between two options to respond to customer pressure on sustainability:
Option 1 — Switch to fully recyclable packaging, raising packaging costs by 8%.
Option 2 — Invest in solar panels on factory roofs, funded by a bank loan.
Justify which option the manufacturer should choose.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
Option 1 (recyclable packaging):
• Visible to customers on every bar — easy to promote and build brand image.
• Responds directly to current consumer pressure.
• Drawback: an 8% rise in packaging cost squeezes margin; may require a price rise.
Option 2 (solar panels):
• Reduces energy bills long term, improving profit once installed.
• Cuts carbon emissions, protecting against future regulation.
• Drawback: loan repayments strain cash flow; payback period may be several years; invisible to customers unless marketed.

Justification must pick one option and weigh it against the other. A strong answer could argue that recyclable packaging is the better short-term move because it is visible to customers and responds to current pressure, while solar panels can be phased in later from retained profit. A different strong answer could argue solar panels deliver larger long-term savings.

Mastering: clear decision with two developed reasons, weighed against the rejected option, applied to the manufacturer.
Secure: decision with one developed reason, supporting point, and some weighing.
Developing: decision stated with limited reasoning or weak weighing.
Emerging: lists pros and cons of both options with no clear decision.
[9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘Ethical behaviour always reduces a business’s profits.’
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
Arguments in support:
• Ethical decisions often raise costs — fair-trade ingredients, higher wages, audited supply chains — squeezing margins.
• Sustainable packaging and cleaner technology require upfront investment before any returns.
• If rivals do not follow suit, ethical firms can be undercut on price.

Arguments against:
• Strong ethical reputation builds customer loyalty, allowing premium pricing (e.g. Patagonia, Tony’s Chocolonely).
• Ethical firms avoid scandals that wipe billions off share prices — Volkswagen (2015), Boohoo (2020).
• Ethical firms attract and retain better staff, cutting recruitment and training costs.
• Early compliance with future regulation avoids scramble and fines later.

Conclusion should introduce a new weighting — for example, it depends on the time frame and the type of customer. In the short term, ethics can reduce profit; in the long term, it often supports profit. The most important factor is whether customers are willing to pay for ethics.

Mastering: balanced argument with two developed points on each side and a justified conclusion that introduces a new weighting.
Secure: balanced argument with some development and a clear conclusion.
Developing: one-sided argument or conclusion that only summarises earlier points.
Emerging: brief points with no real evaluation or conclusion.
[12 marks]

lessons.title: The Economic Climate
lessons.description: How interest rates, employment levels and consumer spending change what UK businesses can do.
lessons.content_html:
What is the Economic Climate?

No business trades in a bubble. The economic climate is the background weather for every decision: whether to take out a loan, hire more staff, launch a premium product or hold off investing. In 2022–2024 the Bank of England lifted interest rates from 0.1% to 5.25% to fight inflation. Every business in the UK felt the change — some sharply.

Key Fact

Three economic forces influence almost every business decision: interest rates (the cost of borrowing), levels of employment (how easy it is to find workers and customers) and consumer spending (how much customers are willing and able to spend).

Interest Rates — the Cost of Money

An interest rate is the price of borrowing money. When rates rise, loans and overdrafts become more expensive. A small bakery that took out a £50,000 loan at 3% might see its monthly repayments jump when it refinances at 7%. That extra cost has to come from somewhere — higher prices, fewer new hires, or delayed expansion plans.

Rising rates also hit customers. Homeowners on variable-rate mortgages pay more each month, leaving less to spend on restaurants, clothes and holidays. In 2023 UK retailers like Wilko collapsed partly because squeezed households pulled back on non-essential shopping. Falling rates have the opposite effect — cheap borrowing encourages spending, investment and house moves.

Higher rates raise the cost of borrowing for investment — new machinery, a new shop, a fleet of delivery vans. A project that gave a 6% return is still worth doing when borrowing costs 3%, but makes no sense at 7%. Businesses delay, scale back, or cancel expansion plans.

Firms that rely on overdrafts to cover day-to-day cash flow see their costs rise month after month. Lower rates reverse this: borrowing feels cheap, investment rises, and the business may hire more staff or launch new products.

Level of Employment

The level of employment is how many people are in work. When employment is high, most people have income to spend — good news for retailers, leisure firms and restaurants. But high employment also means it is harder for businesses to find staff, so wages rise. Cafés and care homes in parts of the UK have faced exactly this: Help Wanted signs in every window, and kitchen staff wages pushed up sharply.

When unemployment rises, the pattern flips. It becomes easier to recruit, and wage growth slows — but consumers have less money overall, so revenue can fall. A recession that puts thousands out of work hits supermarkets at the premium end (Waitrose) and boosts value chains (Aldi, Lidl, B&M) as customers trade down.

When unemployment is low, firms compete for workers. JD Wetherspoon, Greene King and many hospitality chains have raised starting wages, offered sign-on bonuses and invested in training just to fill vacancies. These costs squeeze profit margins unless they can be passed on in higher menu prices.

Some firms respond by automating — self-checkout tills at Tesco, order-at-table apps at Wetherspoon, AI chatbots for customer service. These replace some jobs but save on wage costs in the long run.

Consumer Spending

Consumer spending is the total value of goods and services households buy. It rises when people feel confident, have jobs, low interest rates and rising incomes. It falls when any of these reverse. During the cost-of-living squeeze of 2022–2024, UK consumer spending on non-essentials fell sharply — Domino’s reported fewer orders, cinema visits dipped, and holiday bookings shortened.

Demand for different products reacts differently. Essentials — bread, milk, energy — hold up because everyone needs them. Luxuries — holidays, new cars, designer clothes — are the first to be cut. This is why Poundland and Greggs often do well when economies are weak, while car dealerships and high-end restaurants suffer.

Key Fact

When consumer spending rises, most businesses benefit — but the biggest winners are those selling luxuries. When spending falls, essential and discount retailers (Aldi, Lidl, Poundland) tend to gain market share as customers trade down.

Linking It All Together

The three forces interact. Rising interest rates are usually designed to slow spending; that can reduce demand, which can reduce employment, which can weaken incomes and reduce spending further. For a business, the question is not just ‘what are rates today?’ but ‘how will my customers, my staff and my costs react as the cycle turns?’ Firms that watch these signals can move early — cut costs, change product mix, delay investment — and come out stronger.
lessons.exam_tip_html: You do not need to know how the Bank of England decides interest rates — the focus is on the effect on businesses. For Analyse questions, chain the reasoning: ‘rates rise, so borrowing costs go up, so investment is delayed, so output stays flat.’ For 12-mark Evaluate questions, remember different types of business react differently — luxury retailers suffer more than essential retailers. A conclusion that says ‘it depends on the type of product’ introduces a new weighting rather than repeating earlier points.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Rising interest rates raise the cost of loans and overdrafts and cut customer spending — falling rates do the opposite.
  • High employment means more customers with money but harder (and pricier) recruitment; high unemployment means cheaper labour but weaker demand.
  • Consumer spending is the pulse of demand — essentials hold up in downturns, luxuries suffer; value retailers often gain market share.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the likely impact of a rise in consumer spending on a UK high-street clothing retailer.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (accept developed reasoning that draws on one or more factors):
• Revenue: higher spending means customers buy more items per visit, which raises revenue.
• Margin: confidence lets the retailer hold prices or launch premium ranges, improving profit per sale.
• Investment: stronger cash flow supports opening new stores or refurbishing existing ones, which can lift future sales further.
• Competition: rivals also benefit, so success depends on keeping a clear point of difference (brand, service, style).
• Staffing: higher demand may mean hiring more staff — in a tight labour market this raises wage costs, partially offsetting the revenue gain.

Mastering: developed chains of reasoning using two or more factors, applied to a clothing retailer.
Secure: a developed chain on one factor plus a supporting point, applied.
Developing: relevant points listed with limited development or weak application.
Emerging: generic statements with no application.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘A rise in interest rates always hurts small UK businesses.’
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
Arguments in support:
• Loans, mortgages and overdrafts cost more, cutting profit for firms that are reliant on borrowing.
• Investment is delayed because fewer projects look worthwhile at higher borrowing costs.
• Customers spend less on non-essentials, so restaurants, cafés, boutiques and leisure firms see demand fall.
• Wage pressure may continue if employment stays high, further squeezing margins.

Arguments against:
• Businesses with cash savings earn more interest, boosting income rather than squeezing it.
• Firms that sell essentials (bread, milk, energy) see little change in demand.
• Discount retailers (Aldi, Lidl, Poundland) tend to gain market share as customers trade down.
• A rise in rates can strengthen the pound, lowering the cost of imported materials for firms that bring in supplies from abroad.

Conclusion should introduce a new weighting — for example, it depends on the type of business and how reliant it is on borrowing. The most important factor is the firm’s cost structure: heavily geared firms suffer, cash-rich firms may benefit.

Mastering: balanced argument with two developed points on each side and a justified conclusion that introduces a new weighting.
Secure: balanced argument with some development and a clear conclusion.
Developing: one-sided argument or conclusion that only summarises earlier points.
Emerging: brief points with no real evaluation or conclusion.
[12 marks]

lessons.title: Globalisation & Exchange Rates
lessons.description: How UK businesses compete in world markets, and why a falling or rising pound changes their plans.
lessons.content_html:
The World Has Shrunk

A pair of Nike trainers is designed in the United States, made in Vietnam, shipped through China, sold in a Manchester JD Sports and tracked on an app built in India. That journey used to be science fiction. It is now routine. Globalisation has turned the whole world into a single marketplace — with opportunities and threats for every UK business.

Key Fact

Three forces have accelerated globalisation: cheaper transport (container shipping, air freight), faster digital communication (email, video calls, e-commerce), and lower trade barriers (fewer tariffs and quotas). UK firms like Dyson, JCB, Burberry and BrewDog sell in dozens of countries.

How UK Businesses Compete Internationally

UK firms cannot compete on cheap labour alone — wages are far lower in many emerging markets. Instead, they compete through three main routes: better designs, higher quality products, and clever pricing that makes quality feel affordable. Dyson built a global brand on engineering and design innovation. JCB sells diggers worldwide on reputation for reliability. Burberry charges premium prices backed by heritage and craftsmanship.

Smaller firms compete too. A Yorkshire tea blender sells through Amazon.com to customers in Texas; a Bristol cycling-kit maker takes orders from Australia through its Shopify store. Digital tools and cheap international delivery have opened export markets that used to require a sales team in each country.

Access to larger markets means higher potential sales — a UK firm reaching 300 million customers in Europe has far more room to grow than one selling only to 67 million Britons. Global supply chains also lower costs. Instead of using only UK materials, firms can buy steel from Germany, circuit boards from Taiwan and packaging from China at the best price.

Specialisation is another gain. Firms focus on what they do best — design, R&D, marketing — and outsource the rest. Economies of scale from global volumes drive unit costs down, which lets them compete on price as well as quality.

UK firms now compete with imports from all over the world — often cheaper due to lower labour costs abroad. British factories closed in large numbers through the 1990s and 2000s because Asian manufacturers undercut them. Globalisation also creates supply-chain risk: the 2021 Ever Given container ship that blocked the Suez Canal held up billions of pounds of goods for a week. The pandemic showed how a shortage of microchips made in Taiwan could halt car production in Sunderland.

Currency swings, political shocks (wars, tariffs, sanctions) and cultural differences (what sells in Japan may flop in Brazil) all add complexity. Firms need to manage risks they never faced when their entire market was local.

Exchange Rates

An exchange rate is simply the price of one currency in another. If £1 = $1.25, then UK goods priced at £100 cost an American customer $125. If the pound strengthens to £1 = $1.40, the same UK goods now cost the American $140. Nothing has changed for the UK firm — but its products suddenly look more expensive abroad.

A useful acronym is SPICED — Strong Pound, Imports Cheaper, Exports Dearer. A weak pound reverses this: imports get more expensive (bad for a UK car plant importing steel), but exports get cheaper for foreign buyers (good for UK whisky sold in the US).

Key Fact

A strong pound makes UK exports dearer for foreign buyers (usually reducing sales) but imports cheaper for UK buyers (usually cutting costs for firms that bring in materials). A weak pound does the opposite.

Who Wins and Who Loses

The impact of an exchange-rate change depends on what a business trades. After the 2016 EU referendum the pound fell sharply. UK tourism boomed as overseas visitors found the country cheap — hotels and attractions benefited. But UK holiday firms taking customers abroad saw costs rise because hotels in Spain and France cost more in sterling. UK whisky exporters gained; UK car makers importing components from the EU lost.

The key skill is spotting which side of the trade the case-study business sits on. Then a chain of reasoning follows: strong pound → UK goods dearer for US buyers → US orders fall → UK revenue drops. Exam answers that just recite ‘strong pound bad for exports’ without applying the rule to the business will lose marks.
lessons.exam_tip_html: You will not be asked to calculate exchange-rate conversions — the focus is on the impact on a business. Read the case study carefully and work out whether the firm is an importer, an exporter, or both. Then build your chain of reasoning in order: ‘pound strengthens → exports dearer in foreign currency → overseas orders fall → UK revenue drops.’ A common slip is to apply the SPICED rule mechanically without checking the direction of trade — a strong pound is actually good news for a business that imports raw materials.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Globalisation has opened new markets and cheaper supply chains for UK businesses, but brought tougher international competition and new supply risks.
  • UK firms compete abroad on design, quality and clever pricing rather than low wages — Dyson, JCB and Burberry show what that looks like at scale.
  • Exchange rates shift costs and prices without the business changing anything: SPICED — Strong Pound, Imports Cheaper, Exports Dearer — is the quick mental check.

practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• Identification: a fall in the pound means it takes more pounds to buy the same amount of euros [1 mark].
• Development: so the cost of imported raw materials rises for the UK manufacturer [1 mark].
• Reasoning: because costs are higher, profit margins are squeezed, and the firm may need to raise prices or absorb the cost, which could reduce competitiveness [1 mark].

Developing: correct identification with limited development.

[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a UK whisky distiller of an increase in overseas demand for its products.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (accept developed reasoning that draws on one or more factors):
• Revenue: higher export sales directly raise revenue, especially valuable given the UK market is mature.
• Unit costs: higher volumes allow economies of scale, reducing cost per bottle and raising margins.
• Investment: extra profit supports reinvestment in new stills, warehousing and marketing abroad.
• Exchange-rate risk: earnings in dollars or euros are exposed to currency swings — a stronger pound later would cut the sterling value of overseas sales.
• Supply risk: the distiller needs to scale up safely or it could lose quality, damaging the premium reputation that drove demand in the first place.

Mastering: developed chains of reasoning using two or more factors, applied to the distiller.
Secure: a developed chain on one factor plus a supporting point, applied.
Developing: relevant points listed with limited development or weak application.
Emerging: generic statements with no application.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A UK cycling-kit manufacturer is deciding how to respond to rising international demand:
Option 1 — Open a small sales office in the United States with local staff.
Option 2 — Expand an e-commerce platform in multiple languages from the UK.
Justify which option the manufacturer should choose.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
Option 1 (sales office):
• Builds local knowledge and customer relationships in a huge market.
• Physical presence can help with returns and customer service.
• Drawback: expensive — office rent, staff wages in dollars, visas; slow to set up.
Option 2 (e-commerce):
• Lower set-up cost and faster to launch; reaches many countries at once.
• Uses data from existing UK site to target marketing abroad.
• Drawback: no physical presence; returns and customer service costs rise as overseas sales grow; exchange-rate risk cuts through to the bottom line.

Justification must pick one option and weigh it against the other. A strong answer might argue that e-commerce is better for a small firm because it spreads risk across many markets with lower capital outlay. A different strong answer might argue the sales office suits a firm with premium products where local presence builds trust.

Mastering: clear decision with two developed reasons, weighed against the rejected option, applied.
Secure: decision with one developed reason, supporting point, and some weighing.
Developing: decision stated with limited reasoning or weak weighing.
Emerging: lists pros and cons of both options with no clear decision.
[9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘Globalisation is more of a threat than an opportunity for small UK businesses.’
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
Arguments in support (threat):
• Small UK firms face tough competition from overseas producers with much lower labour and material costs.
• Supply-chain shocks (Suez Canal, pandemic chip shortages, tariffs) hit small firms hardest because they lack the scale to absorb disruption.
• Exchange-rate swings make costs and revenues unpredictable, and small firms cannot easily hedge.

Arguments against (opportunity):
• E-commerce tools (Shopify, Amazon, Etsy) open global export markets that used to need a sales team in each country.
• Access to cheap overseas suppliers lowers costs for small manufacturers.
• Global platforms (Instagram, TikTok) provide low-cost marketing to customers worldwide.
• A weak pound can make UK exports more competitive abroad, boosting small exporter revenue.

Conclusion should introduce a new weighting — for example, it depends on the type of product and how digitally ready the firm is. The most important factor is probably whether the firm can differentiate on quality, design or niche rather than price.

Mastering: balanced argument with two developed points on each side and a justified conclusion that introduces a new weighting.
Secure: balanced argument with some development and a clear conclusion.
Developing: one-sided argument or conclusion that only summarises earlier points.
Emerging: brief points with no real evaluation or conclusion.
[12 marks]

lessons.title: Legislation & Competition
lessons.description: Employment law, health and safety, consumer law, and how competition and uncertainty shape business decisions.
lessons.content_html:
Playing by the Rules

Every UK business operates inside a framework of laws that tell it how to treat staff, how to keep them safe, and how to treat customers fairly. It also trades in markets where rivals push back on every decision. Legislation is the rulebook. Competition is the opponent. Both influence what a business can charge, how it hires, and how much it must invest.

Key Fact

Three main areas of UK legislation affect businesses directly: employment law (e.g. the Equality Act 2010), health and safety law (e.g. the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974), and consumer law (trade descriptions and consumer rights).

Employment Law

UK employment law protects workers. The National Minimum Wage sets the lowest legal hourly pay, with a higher rate (the National Living Wage) for workers aged 21 and over. Businesses that pay less face fines and public naming by HMRC — as Argos, Superdrug and even Marks & Spencer have all discovered in recent years.

The Equality Act 2010 makes it unlawful to treat people unfairly because of age, disability, gender, race, religion, sexual orientation and other protected characteristics. A business must train managers, adjust recruitment processes and, in some cases, adapt premises. Costs rise, but so does the pool of talent and the protection against costly tribunal cases.

The Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 is the cornerstone law. Employers must provide a safe workplace, train staff, supply protective equipment and carry out risk assessments. A kitchen must keep slip hazards under control; a warehouse must manage forklift risks; an office must have fire drills.

The benefits of compliance are not just legal. Fewer accidents mean less absence, lower insurance premiums and a stronger reputation as a place to work. The cost of ignoring the rules is heavy — fines can run into millions, and, in serious cases, directors can be jailed.

Consumer Law

Consumer law stops businesses from misleading or cheating customers. Trade descriptions rules mean a fridge sold as ‘A-rated energy efficient’ must actually be A-rated. Goods must match their description, be of satisfactory quality and fit for purpose. Services must be provided with reasonable care and skill. Breaking these rules leads to refunds, fines and reputational damage.

Enforcement is serious. Volkswagen paid out huge sums when its cars did not match their emissions description. Ticketing sites and online retailers have been fined for hidden charges. ‘Buy one get one free’ deals must be genuine; a price marked ‘was £50, now £25’ must actually have been £50 recently. Consumer trust, once lost, is expensive to rebuild.

The Cost of Legislation

Following the law costs money: higher wages from minimum-wage rises, training on equality and safety, protective equipment, store and website changes to meet consumer rights, and legal advice. For a small café or independent shop these costs bite proportionally harder than for a large retailer. But the downsides of breaking the rules — fines, compensation, lost customers, tribunal defeats, jail in the worst cases — almost always outweigh any savings.

Key Fact

Legislation raises costs (higher wages, training, equipment) but also brings benefits — fewer accidents, better staff retention, stronger reputation and protection from costly lawsuits. The exam reward is in weighing both sides.

The Competitive Environment

A market is where buyers and sellers come together. In most UK markets, several firms compete for the same customers. Supermarkets fight Tesco, Sainsbury’s, Asda, Morrisons, Aldi and Lidl. Streaming platforms fight Netflix, Disney+, Amazon Prime and Apple TV+. Competition forces firms to improve — lower prices, better quality, stronger service — or lose market share.

Competition is not always fierce. A local corner shop in a rural village may face minimal competition because the next nearest shop is ten miles away. Regulated utilities (water supply) can also have very limited competition. Firms in low-competition markets often enjoy higher prices and easier profits — but they can become lazy, which is why new rivals, when they eventually arrive, can cause a sudden shock.

Every business faces risk — the chance that a decision leads to loss. Risks include new rivals arriving, laws changing, costs rising, customers changing taste, or economies tipping into recession. Uncertainty is broader — the future is unknown, and even careful planning cannot prevent shocks like a pandemic, a war, or a sudden technology change.

Entrepreneurs accept risk because they see the upside. Businesses reduce risk through market research, insurance, diversification, financial reserves, and keeping an eye on the competitive and legal landscape. The goal is not to eliminate risk — that is impossible — but to make smarter, faster decisions than rivals.

Legislation, competition and uncertainty together shape daily life for UK businesses. The firms that thrive are the ones that treat the law as a floor (the minimum expected behaviour), read the competition carefully, and plan for risk rather than pretending it does not exist.
lessons.exam_tip_html: You only need brief knowledge of each law — examiners want you to explain the effect on a business, not recite dates and section numbers. For Analyse and Evaluate questions, pair a cost (higher wages, training, refunds) with a benefit (fewer lawsuits, better reputation, stronger brand). For questions on competition, always link the level of competition to what the business can do with price, product and customer service. A strong conclusion introduces a new weighting — often ‘it depends on the market the business trades in’.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • UK businesses must comply with employment law (minimum wage, Equality Act), health and safety law, and consumer law — each raises costs but protects reputation and people.
  • Competition forces businesses to improve price, quality and service; minimal competition can mean higher profits but also complacency.
  • Every business faces risk and uncertainty; smart firms reduce risk through research, insurance, diversification and careful planning rather than trying to eliminate it.

B) A legal minimum hourly wage

practice_questions.text: Give two ways in which consumer law protects customers when they buy products from a UK business.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for any two of the following:
• Goods must match the description given by the seller [1 mark]
• Goods must be of satisfactory quality [1 mark]
• Goods must be fit for their intended purpose [1 mark]
• Customers have a right to refunds, repairs or replacements for faulty goods [1 mark]
• Adverts must not be misleading (trade descriptions) [1 mark]

Mastering: two precise, separate protections using correct business vocabulary.
Secure: two correct protections.
Developing: one correct protection; second vague or repeated.

[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way a rise in the National Minimum Wage could affect a small restaurant.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• Identification: the restaurant’s wage bill rises because it must pay every eligible employee more per hour [1 mark].
• Development: this cuts the profit margin on every meal served unless prices are raised [1 mark].
• Reasoning: so the owner may have to increase menu prices, which could reduce demand, or cut back on staff hours, which could affect service quality and customer satisfaction [1 mark].

Mastering: identification, development AND a ‘because’ chain of reasoning.
Secure: identification and clear development.
Developing: correct identification with limited development.
Emerging: vague or incorrect point.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a UK supermarket of increased competition from a new discount rival opening nearby.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (accept developed reasoning that draws on one or more factors):
• Price: the supermarket may cut prices on key lines to protect market share, which squeezes profit margin.
• Product: it may expand its own-brand value range to match the discounter, taking shelf space from premium lines.
• Promotion: more spending on loyalty schemes (Clubcard, Nectar) to lock in existing customers.
• Service: improved in-store experience (cleaner stores, longer opening hours, faster checkouts) to offer something the discounter does not.
• Risk: if it cannot match the discounter on price, it risks losing customers who trade down, especially during a cost-of-living squeeze.

Mastering: developed chains of reasoning using two or more factors, applied to the supermarket.
Secure: a developed chain on one factor plus a supporting point, applied.
Developing: relevant points listed with limited development or weak application.
Emerging: generic statements with no application.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A UK builder is deciding how to respond to a tightening of health and safety enforcement on construction sites:
Option 1 — Invest in new safety equipment and full training for all site staff.
Option 2 — Hire a specialist health-and-safety consultant to review and improve procedures without buying new equipment.
Justify which option the builder should choose.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
Option 1 (equipment and training):
• Directly reduces accident risk on site — protects workers and the business’s reputation.
• Training means every worker is aware of updated rules, reducing liability.
• Drawback: significant upfront cost; new equipment may be underused if practices do not change.
Option 2 (consultant):
• Cheaper in the short term — no large equipment bill.
• A specialist brings wider industry experience and can redesign procedures.
• Drawback: advice is only as good as the implementation; without investment in equipment some hazards remain.

Justification must choose one option and weigh it against the other. A strong answer might argue that equipment plus training is worth the investment because accidents on construction sites can kill and fines are huge, so prevention is cheaper than cure. A different strong answer might argue the consultant-first approach is sensible because it identifies priorities before spending money.

Mastering: clear decision with two developed reasons, weighed against the rejected option, applied.
Secure: decision with one developed reason, supporting point, and some weighing.
Developing: decision stated with limited reasoning or weak weighing.
Emerging: lists pros and cons of both options with no clear decision.
[9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘The more laws that apply to a business, the harder it is to make a profit.’
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
Arguments in support:
• Employment laws raise wage bills through the minimum wage, pensions auto-enrolment and holiday pay.
• Health and safety compliance requires training, equipment, risk assessments and record keeping — all costly.
• Consumer law means refunds, recalls and restrictions on advertising, adding cost and limiting marketing.
• Small firms carry the relative burden most heavily because compliance costs are similar but revenues are smaller.

Arguments against:
• Laws create a level playing field — rivals cannot cut corners to undercut compliant firms.
• Compliant businesses avoid fines, lawsuits and brand-damaging scandals (e.g. the supplier-wage scandals at Boohoo).
• Better-treated staff are more motivated, reducing turnover and training costs — which supports profit.
• Safer workplaces mean fewer accidents, lower insurance, and less lost production.
• Laws can attract ethical customers and staff, building reputation.

Conclusion should introduce a new weighting — for example, it depends on the size and type of business. For a small new firm, compliance cost may be a heavy burden in year one; for an established firm, the costs are usually outweighed by reputational gain and risk reduction. The most important factor is how well the business plans for compliance before it becomes a problem.

Mastering: balanced argument with two developed points on each side and a justified conclusion that introduces a new weighting.
Secure: balanced argument with some development and a clear conclusion.
Developing: one-sided argument or conclusion that only summarises earlier points.
Emerging: brief points with no real evaluation or conclusion.
[12 marks]

glossary_terms.definition: Laws passed by Parliament that businesses must follow, covering areas such as employment, health and safety, and consumer protection.
A UK law setting the lowest legal hourly pay for workers, with a higher rate called the National Living Wage for workers aged 21 and over.
Laws that protect customers, requiring goods to match their description, be of satisfactory quality and fit for purpose.
